entry: Branch of medicine concerned with the medical care of [[Infant|infants]], [[Child|children]] and young adults. In the Commonwealth, pediatric care covers patients up to age 18, and in India up to age 12; the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends care through age 21. A physician who specializes in the field is a pediatrician. Ancient writers addressed childhood disease, including epilepsy and premature births, in the [[Hippocrates|Hippocratic Corpus]] of the fifth century BC. The Persian physician al-Razi, sometimes called the father of pediatrics, wrote *Diseases in Children*. Among the first books on the subject was Paolo Bagellardo's *Libellus de aegritudinibus et remediis infantium* (1472), by an Italian pediatrician. Specialized care for children developed in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the Swedish physician Nils Rosén von Rosenstein is considered the founder of pediatrics as a medical specialty.

Sexual attraction to prepubescent children, classified as a [[Paraphilia|paraphilia]]. In the DSM-5 and ICD-11, pedophilic disorder means a pattern of pedophilic arousal that causes distress or interpersonal difficulty, or that a person has acted on. The DSM-5 requires that the person be at least 16 years old and at least five years older than the children, and that the pattern last six months or longer; the ICD-11 gives no chronological ages. Pedophilia is not the same as [[Child sexual abuse|child sexual abuse]]: not all abusers are pedophiles, and many pedophiles never molest children. The condition was first formally recognized in the late 19th century, and research has grown since the 1980s. No cure has been developed, though therapies can reduce the risk that a person acts on attraction. The causes have not been conclusively established.

Outermost layer of the Earth, made up of [[Soil|soil]]. The name comes from Ancient Greek words for "ground" and "sphere." The pedosphere lies at the interface of the [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]], atmosphere, [[Hydrosphere|hydrosphere]] and [[Biosphere|biosphere]], and it is the foundation of terrestrial ecosystems. It mediates the chemical and biogeochemical flows between these systems. Soil formation begins when [[Weathering|weathering]] breaks down rock; biology speeds the process, with lichens, mosses and seed-bearing plants among the pioneers, and their secreted acids help break rock apart. The soil layer is typically 1–2 meters thick and holds approximately 2,500 gigatons of organic carbon, over three times the atmospheric amount. The term was coined in 1938 by Swedish soil chemist Sante Mattson.

Spanish dramatist and poet of the Golden Age. Born into minor nobility in [[Madrid|Madrid]], Calderón served as a soldier and as a [[Knight|knight]] of the Order of Santiago before becoming a Roman Catholic priest. His theatrical debut, a history play about [[Edward III|King Edward III]] of England, was performed in 1623 at the Royal Alcázar of Madrid. He wrote many verse dramas, including mystery plays for the Feast of Corpus Christi and comedies and tragedies built on the honor code of the Spanish nobility. His masterpiece, *La vida es sueño* (*Life Is a Dream*), explores whether fate is written in advance or can be changed by [[Free will|free will]]. Building on conventions set by [[Lope de Vega|Lope de Vega]], he pioneered techniques later termed metafiction and surrealism, and his influence extends to [[Romanticism|Romanticism]] and dystopian [[Science fiction|science fiction]].

[[Empire of Brazil|Emperor of Brazil]] (1831–89). Pedro became emperor at age five after his father's abdication, and a regency governed until he assumed personal rule in 1840. His reign, the longest and most stable in Brazilian history, saw Brazil achieve military success in conflicts such as the Platine War, the Uruguayan War and the [[Paraguayan War]]. He promoted education, science and culture, and despite resistance from powerful interests he supported and enabled the abolition of slavery in 1888. A military coup in 1889 deposed him, led mainly by officers who favored a republic. He went into exile in Europe without resisting and died of [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] in Paris. His remains were later returned to Brazil with national honors, and many historians rank him among the greatest statesmen in Brazilian history.

Founder of the [[Empire of Brazil]] (1822–31) and king of Portugal (1826). Pedro was born in [[Lisbon]], the son of King John VI of Portugal. The royal family fled to Brazil after French troops invaded Portugal in 1807. When the Liberal Revolution of 1820 forced John VI back to Portugal in 1821, Pedro governed Brazil as regent. On September 7, 1822, he declared Brazil's independence from Portugal, and in October he was acclaimed emperor. The Cisplatine War cost Brazil the province of Cisplatina, and disputes over the balance of power between monarch and parliament weakened his rule. He abdicated in April 1831 in favor of his five-year-old son, Pedro II. In 1832 he invaded Portugal at the head of an army, becoming part of a wider conflict across the [[Iberian Peninsula]] between liberals and absolutists. He died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] a few months after the liberals' victory.

Spanish politician, prime minister since 2018. A member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), he has been the party's secretary-general since 2017. In June 2018 the PSOE won a vote of no confidence against Mariano Rajoy, backed by Unidas Podemos and regionalist parties, and Sánchez became prime minister. After winning the most votes in November 2019, he formed a minority coalition with Unidas Podemos, the first national coalition government since the return to democracy. After a snap general election in 2023 he formed another coalition and was appointed to a third term on November 17, 2023.

Portuguese navigator regarded as the European discoverer of [[Brazil|Brazil]]. In 1500 Cabral led a fleet of 13 ships to India along the route opened by [[Vasco da Gama|Vasco da Gama]]. Sailing far into the Atlantic, he made landfall in April 1500 on what he first took to be a large island. Because the land lay within Portugal's sphere under the [[Treaty of Tordesillas|Treaty of Tordesillas]], he claimed it for Portugal; it later came to be known as Brazil. He led the first known expedition to touch four continents. Storms sank several ships in the South Atlantic. After an attack on the Portuguese at Calicut, Cabral bombarded the city; at Cochin he loaded spices before returning to Europe, where the profits helped finance the Portuguese Crown. Emperor [[Pedro II of Brazil|Pedro II]] later rehabilitated Cabral's reputation, and historians consider him a major figure of the [[Age of Discovery|Age of Discovery]].

Influence exerted by members of a social group on their peers to conform to the group's attitudes, values or behavior. Peers are people with similar interests, experiences or social status. Members of a peer group are more likely to influence a person's beliefs, values, religion and behavior, and the effect may be positive or negative. A person need not belong to a group to be affected, and organizations as well as individuals can be susceptible. Peer pressure ranges from subtle disapproval to threats and physical violence. It affects all ethnic groups, genders and ages, but it has been studied most among [[Child|children]] and [[Adolescence|adolescents]], who are trying to find identity and belonging. For adolescents, research has focused on sexual activity and substance abuse. It occurs face-to-face and through [[Social media|social media]].

Evaluation of work by people of similar expertise to its producers. Peer review functions as self-regulation by qualified members of a profession and is used to maintain quality standards, improve performance and provide credibility. In academia, scholarly peer review decides whether a paper is suitable for publication; reviewers are anonymous experts on the topic, and top journals reject over 90% of submitted papers. Henry Oldenburg, a German-born British philosopher, is seen as the "father" of modern scientific peer review. The journal [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] made it standard practice in 1973, and the term came into use in the early 1970s.

Winged horse of Greek mythology, usually depicted as a white stallion. Several accounts say that he was sired by [[Poseidon|Poseidon]] and born from the blood of [[Medusa|Medusa]] when [[Perseus|Perseus]] beheaded her. The hero Bellerophon captured him near the spring Peirene, and Pegasus helped him defeat the [[Chimera (mythology)|Chimera]]. When Bellerophon tried to ride him up to [[Mount Olympus|Mount Olympus]], the hero fell, and Pegasus continued alone. In later accounts [[Zeus|Zeus]] takes Pegasus to Olympus to carry his thunderbolts. Where his hoof struck Mount Helicon, the spring Hippocrene appeared, and it was linked to the [[Muses|Muses]]. Pegasus is also a constellation and a frequent subject of ancient Greek pottery and Renaissance art.

Public university in Haidian, Beijing, China. Founded in 1898 as the Imperial University of Peking by charter of the Guangxu Emperor, it is the second-oldest university in China after Tianjin University. It was renamed Peking University in 1912 under the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]]. It merged with Yenching University in 1952 and with Beijing Medical University in 2000. Under president Cai Yuanpei from 1917, it adopted faculty governance and academic freedom, and it recruited progressive scholars including [[Lu Xun|Lu Xun]] and Hu Shih. In 1919 students here protested the [[Treaty of Versailles|Treaty of Versailles]], sparking the May Fourth Movement. The university is funded by the Ministry of Education and is a member of the C9 League.

Dominant form of Chinese opera, combining music, vocal performance, mime, martial arts, dance and acrobatics. It arose in [[Beijing|Beijing]] in the mid-[[Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]], when Anhui troupes performed there in 1790 for the [[Qianlong Emperor|Qianlong Emperor]]'s birthday, and Hubei troupes joined them in 1828. It was fully developed by the mid-19th century. Its four main role types are shēng ("gentlemen"), dàn ("women"), jìng ("rough men") and chǒu ("clowns"). Performers are judged by the beauty of their movements on a sparse stage, and the music uses the xīpí and èrhuáng styles. The repertoire includes over 1,400 works. Denounced during the [[Cultural Revolution|Cultural Revolution]], the art was largely restored afterward, and UNESCO inscribed it on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2010.

Brazilian soccer player, widely regarded as one of the greatest in history. Born Edson Arantes do Nascimento, he played as a forward, starting for Santos at age 15 and for Brazil at 16. He won three [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]] titles, in 1958, 1962 and 1970, becoming the only player to do so and the youngest winner at age 17. Nicknamed "O Rei" ("the King") after 1958, he scored 77 goals in 92 games for Brazil and 643 goals in 659 games for Santos. He led Santos to victory in the [[Copa Libertadores|Copa Libertadores]] in 1962 and 1963. In 1999 the International Olympic Committee named him Athlete of the Century, and he shared the FIFA Player of the Century award with [[Diego Maradona|Diego Maradona]]. He retired in 1977.

Genus of large water birds with a long bill and a throat pouch. The eight living species have a patchy but global distribution, from the tropics to temperate zones, and are absent from polar regions and the open ocean. Pelicans feed mainly on fish, which they catch by diving or scooping and then drain of water in the pouch before swallowing. They are gregarious, hunting in flocks and breeding in colonies; four white species tend to nest on the ground, and four brown or gray species mainly in trees. Once thought to be related to [[Frigatebird|frigatebirds]] and [[Cormorant|cormorants]], pelicans are placed in the order Pelecaniformes and are most closely related to the [[Shoebill|shoebill]] and hamerkop. The genus was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758. Populations have declined through habitat destruction, disturbance and pollution, and three species are of conservation concern.

Conflict (431–404 BC) between the [[Delian League|Athenian-led Delian League]] and the Spartan-led Peloponnesian League. It was fought for hegemony over ancient Greece. It began in 431 BC when the Spartan king Archidamus II invaded Attica, and the Peace of Nicias was signed in 421 BC. The Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BC) ended in Athenian defeat and the loss of most of Athens's navy. [[Sparta|Sparta]], allied with Persia, renewed the war in 413 BC, and its Persian-financed fleet won the decisive battle of Aegospotami in 405 BC. Athens fell in 404 BC, the Delian League was dissolved, and Sparta installed oligarchies, including the Thirty Tyrants in Athens. The war ended Athens's empire and maritime dominance, impoverished much of the Peloponnese, and made civil war between democratic and oligarchic factions common. The main source is the history by [[Thucydides|Thucydides]].

Lower part of the trunk, between the [[Abdomen|abdomen]] and the thighs, together with its embedded skeleton. The bony pelvis is formed by the sacrum and coccyx and two hip bones, each made of the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse during puberty. The hip bones connect the spine to the lower limbs at the hip joints. The pelvic cavity, enclosed by the bones, mainly contains the reproductive organs and rectum, and the pelvic floor supports the abdominal organs while controlling the openings of the rectum and urogenital organs. In mammals the bony pelvis is larger in females, allowing offspring to pass through it at birth. The female pelvis is broader, with a subpubic angle greater than 80 degrees, while the male pelvis is narrower, with an angle less than 70 degrees.

Writing and drawing instrument that applies ink to a surface, typically paper. Early pens, including reed, quill and dip pens, held ink on a nib and had to be recharged from an [[Ink|inkwell]]. Modern pens, such as ballpoint, rollerball, fountain and felt-tip pens, have internal ink reservoirs. Ancient Egyptians wrote on [[Papyrus|papyrus]] with reed pens, and quills, made from feathers, were widely used from about the 7th century. Quill pens were used to write and sign the [[Constitution of the United States|Constitution of the United States]] in 1787. Metal-nibbed pens were mass-produced in [[Birmingham|Birmingham]], England, from 1822. The ballpoint pen was developed in 1938 by Hungarian journalist László Bíró.

Spanish actress who works in Spanish- and English-language films. She won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Supporting Actress for her role in [[Woody Allen|Woody Allen]]'s *Vicky Cristina Barcelona* (2008). She has appeared in seven films directed by Pedro Almodóvar, including *Live Flesh* (1997), *All About My Mother* (1999) and *Volver* (2006). Her other awards include a BAFTA Award and three Goya Awards.

Malaysian state on Penang Island and the Seberang Perai mainland (pop., 2020: 1.74 million). The state lies on the northwest coast of Peninsular Malaysia, and its capital, George Town, is on Penang Island. Francis Light, an agent of the British [[East India Company|East India Company]], obtained the island from the sultan of Kedah in 1786 in exchange for military aid and established a free port there. Penang later became part of the Straits Settlements, which also included Malacca and [[Singapore|Singapore]]. Japan occupied it during [[World War II|World War II]] until the British regained control in 1945. Penang's economy shifted from trade to electronics manufacturing in the late 20th century. It is Malaysia's most densely populated state, at 1,659 per sq km, and it is culturally diverse, with Chinese, Malay, Indian, Eurasian and Siamese communities.

Writing and drawing implement with a solid pigment core in a protective casing. Pencils make marks by abrasion, leaving a trail of core material on paper. Most cores are graphite mixed with [[Clay|clay]], which makes erasable gray or black marks. [[Charcoal|Charcoal]] cores are used mainly for sketching, and grease pencils mark smooth surfaces such as glass. The most common casing is hexagonal wood bonded to the core, which must be peeled to expose the point. Mechanical pencils have separate cores that can be extended and reloaded. Graphite was found in large deposits in Borrowdale, England, in the 16th century and was first wrapped in string or sheepskin. In 1795 French army officer Nicolas-Jacques Conté developed a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay, forming rods and firing them, which enabled mass production. The core is called "lead," though it contains no lead.

Weight suspended from a pivot so that it swings freely under [[Gravity|gravity]]. When displaced from its equilibrium position, a pendulum is pulled back toward it and oscillates. The period, the time for one complete cycle, depends on the pendulum's length and, slightly, on the amplitude of its swing, but not on the mass of the bob. For small swings the period is nearly constant, a property called isochronism that makes pendulums useful for timekeeping. [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] observed isochronism in 1602. [[Christiaan Huygens|Christiaan Huygens]] invented the pendulum clock in 1656, and it was the world's standard timekeeper for several centuries. [[Quartz|Quartz]] clocks superseded it as a time standard in the 1930s. Pendulums are also used in seismometers and accelerometers, and in the [[Foucault pendulum|Foucault pendulum]], which demonstrates Earth's rotation.

Flightless, semi-aquatic sea bird found almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere. Penguins have countershaded dark and white plumage and flippers for swimming. They feed on [[Krill|krill]], fish and [[Squid|squid]], which they swallow whole. Only one species, the Galapagos penguin, lives at or slightly north of the equator. The largest living species is the [[Emperor penguin|emperor penguin]], about 1.1 m tall and 35 kg in weight. The smallest is the little blue penguin, which stands 30–33 cm tall. Some prehistoric species were as tall or heavy as an adult human. The word first appeared in English in the late 16th century as a synonym for the [[Great auk|great auk]], a Northern Hemisphere bird to which penguins are not closely related.

Group of [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]] originally obtained from Penicillium molds. Most penicillins in clinical use are produced by fermenting *Penicillium chrysogenum* in deep tanks. Penicillin G, given intramuscularly or intravenously, and penicillin V, taken by mouth, are the two purified forms in clinical use. Penicillins were among the first drugs effective against many staphylococcal and streptococcal infections, and they remain widely used, although many [[Bacteria|bacteria]] have developed resistance. [[Alexander Fleming|Alexander Fleming]] discovered penicillin in 1928 as a crude extract of *Penicillium rubens*. A team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain at the [[University of Oxford|University of Oxford]] isolated the purified compound in 1940. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Semisynthetic penicillins later broadened the range of bacteria they can treat.

Landform that extends from a mainland, is connected to it on one side and is mostly surrounded by water. Peninsulas exist on every continent, and the largest is the [[Arabian Peninsula|Arabian Peninsula]], at approximately 3.2 million sq km. The connection to the mainland may be an [[Isthmus|isthmus]], such as the Isthmus of Corinth linking the Peloponnese to central Greece. Peninsulas form through continental drift, glacial erosion and deposition, volcanic eruptions, river sediment and rifting at [[Plate tectonics|plate boundaries]]. Changes in water level can turn a peninsula into an island at high water and make it smaller in dry weather. Peninsulas have sheltered prehistoric humans and Neanderthals, who could hunt both land and sea animals, and they have been important for trade through their access to water.
